text: cin infusion may be used to maintain uterine contraction.3 Prostaglan- dins such as carboprost or dinoprostone may be used for primary postpartum haemorrhage1,2 that has not been con- trolled by oxytocin and ergot preparations.3 Rectal misopr- ostol has also been shown to be effective,4 but a subse- quent review5 found that the original study was not large enough to evaluate the effects on maternal mortality, seri- ous morbidity, or hysterectomy rates, and that there was insufficient evidence to support the use of misoprostol in- stead of a combination of oxytocin and ergometrine. How- ever, there is considerable interest in the use of misopros- tol, particularly for developing countries, because of its better stability and ease of administration;3 further re- search has been encouraged.6,7 Surgery may be required if medical management does not control bleeding.2,3 Secondary postpartum haemorrhage occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks after delivery and although associated with maternal morbidity rather than death in developed countries, it is a major contributor to maternal death in de- veloping countries. Antibacterials, oxytocics, hormone therapy, and a variety of surgical treatments are used,1,2,8 but a systematic review8 concluded that evidence for the best treatment is lacking. Risk factors for postpartum haemorrhage include pro- longed labour, augmented labour, overdistended uterus (for example in multiple pregnancy), and a history of post- partum haemorrhage.2 However, atonic postpartum haem- orrhage occurs in many women without identifiable risk factors, and authorities recommend that prophylaxis should be offered to all women during childbirth.9,10 Active management of the third stage of labour involves prophy- lactic use of an oxytocic, cord clamping before placental delivery, controlled cord traction, and uterine massage af- ter delivery of the placenta. The routine use of active management, with oxytocics usually given after delivery of the anterior shoulder or im- mediately after delivery of the baby, reduces blood loss, the risk of postpartum haemorrhage, and the risk of pro- longed third stage of labour.11 However, despite the wide- spread use of oxytocics there is limited evidence of high quality comparing different drugs.
